section_summary: This section gathers records on strategic materials and wartime trade with Japan, including prewar U.S. exports of arms, scrap iron, petroleum, and magnesium; Swedish machinery exports; and public and congressional inquiries into export controls. It also covers procedures for confiscating and evaluating captured Japanese weapons, Japanese requisitioning of metal in occupied China, and offers of Japanese industrial catalogues to U.S. intelligence. The final pages contain a major intelligence report, with detailed tables, on Japanese armaments production in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria during 1942 and the influence of a German technical mission.

subfiles.title: Request for change of classification for Despatch No. 758
subfiles.to: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Requests review of the confidential classification of a 1942 Chungking despatch on Chinese trade in strategic materials with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The form identifies Despatch No. 758 of November 27, 1942, from the American Embassy at Chungking, with an enclosure by John S. Service. Stephen A. Comiskey authorized retention or review of its classification on April 11, 1956.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Congresswoman Rankin’s request for Japanese export statistics
subfiles.about: Records Jeannette Rankin’s request for statistics and an explanation of U.S. economic measures against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rankin asked for annual figures on exports to Japan of arms, scrap iron, and petroleum products from 1937 through 1941. The memorandum also notes discussion of the moral embargoes, the National Defense Act of July 2, 1940, and the July 1941 asset-freezing measures.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting export statistics to Jeannette Rankin
subfiles.about: Transmits a memorandum on U.S. exports of arms, scrap iron, and petroleum products to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department responds to Rankin’s oral request by enclosing statistics for 1937–1940. The three categories are arms and implements of war, scrap iron, and petroleum products.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of U.S. exports of arms, scrap iron, and petroleum to Japan
subfiles.about: Provides detailed statistics on licensed arms exports and U.S. scrap and petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum compares arms-export licences and actual shipments to China and Japan from 1937 through 1941. It then measures Japanese purchases of iron and steel scrap against total U.S. exports and consumption. A final table covers crude petroleum, gasoline, fuel oil, lubricating oil, and kerosene during 1937–1940.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on a North China iron-smelting company
subfiles.about: Refers researchers to a Chungking telegram on Japanese establishment of an iron-smelting company in North China.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Telegram No. 1518 of December 18, 1942, from Chungking. The original was filed under a separate economic file number.

subfiles.title: Departmental note on Swedish machinery exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes Swedish information that no specified machinery or automotive parts were exported to Japan or occupied territories in 1942.
subfiles.summary: The note says earlier exports had included a substantial but declining volume of ball and roller bearings. Grinding machines were shipped in smaller quantities, while other requested items were insignificant.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1081 on Swedish machinery exports to Japan, first copy
subfiles.from: Winthrop S. Greene, American Legation, Stockholm
subfiles.about: Reports Swedish exports of machinery, bearings, motors, and related equipment to Japan and Japanese-occupied territories.
subfiles.summary: The despatch supplies State Trade Commission statistics for 1935–1941 and reports no exports during 1942. It identifies major Swedish manufacturers and agency houses involved in Far Eastern trade, while noting that the Foreign Office would not disclose individual shippers and consignees. The enclosure tabulates exports by commodity and destination.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1081 on Swedish machinery exports to Japan, duplicate copy
subfiles.from: Winthrop S. Greene, American Legation, Stockholm
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the report and tables on Swedish industrial exports to Japan and occupied Asian territories.
subfiles.summary: Greene discusses bearings from SKF, centerless grinders, small-craft motors, and the agency houses handling much of Sweden’s trade with East Asia. He also clarifies the products manufactured by Svenska Turbinfabriks A.B. Ljungström. The enclosed table gives annual values for bearings, motors, machine tools, transmissions, gears, and automotive parts.

subfiles.title: Clarence F. Lea’s inquiry about title to a captured Japanese field gun
subfiles.about: Seeks advice on allowing a merchant captain to retain a damaged Japanese 75-mm field piece for public display.
subfiles.summary: Lea forwards a letter from R. W. Look, master of the S.S. Peter Silvester. He asks how Look might obtain legal title, what other captured articles could be brought into the United States, and whether the gun could eventually be returned after military examination.

subfiles.title: R. W. Look’s request concerning captured Japanese materiel
subfiles.about: Requests assistance in donating a captured Japanese field piece to Sausalito for display.
subfiles.summary: Look explains that he is carrying scrap metal as ballast from New Caledonia to San Francisco. A damaged Japanese 75-mm field piece was given to him at a captured artillery dump, but he regards his title as inadequate and seeks War Department authorization to give it to Sausalito.

subfiles.title: Meeting on importation of captured enemy materiel
subfiles.about: Records an interdepartmental policy meeting on captured enemy weapons and other materiel entering U.S. ports.
subfiles.summary: Army, Navy, Customs, and State representatives classified imports as official shipments, merchant-seamen acquisitions, service members’ souvenirs, or parcel-post shipments. Significant materiel was to be seized by Customs and sent to Aberdeen for intelligence examination, while harmless souvenirs could often be returned. The Japanese field gun intended for Sausalito would be transferred to the Army, with ownership claims deferred until after the war.

subfiles.title: Reply to Clarence F. Lea on the captured Japanese field piece
subfiles.about: Explains the new policy requiring captured enemy materiel to be examined by Army or Navy intelligence.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that enemy material acquired by capture, purchase, barter, or battlefield recovery is important to military intelligence. Customs will hold such articles pending an Army or Navy decision, and Lea is advised to refer the gun’s eventual disposition to Army Ordnance Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Bern concerning a Japanese mercury purchase
subfiles.about: Requests investigation of a reported Japanese effort to buy mercury through a Spanish mission in Zürich.
subfiles.summary: The message says a Japanese delegation was negotiating for mercury and that Crédit Suisse was handling a transaction involving blocked Swiss francs and 2.5 million pesetas. Bern was asked how the financing would work and how the transaction might be disrupted.

subfiles.title: Bern reply on the reported mercury transaction
subfiles.about: Reports that no information beyond the military attaché’s original account of the mercury deal was yet available.
subfiles.summary: The Legation says the matter remained under investigation. It promises to transmit any additional particulars promptly.

subfiles.title: Charles K. Clark’s request to import captured Japanese weapons
subfiles.about: Asks permission to bring captured Japanese machine guns, a rifle, and other articles into the United States.
subfiles.summary: The badly degraded letter concerns weapons taken from Japanese forces on Guadalcanal. Later correspondence identifies the articles as three machine guns and a rifle and shows that Clark sought clearance to retain them as personal property.

subfiles.title: Letter to San Francisco Customs concerning Charles K. Clark
subfiles.from: Frederick Exton, Division of Commercial Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards Clark’s request and the Department’s response concerning captured Japanese weapons.
subfiles.summary: Exton encloses Clark’s April 17 letter about three machine guns, a rifle, and other articles. He also supplies Customs with a copy of the Department’s reply to Clark.

subfiles.title: Reply to Charles K. Clark on captured weapons
subfiles.from: Frederick Exton, Division of Commercial Affairs
subfiles.about: Advises Clark that Customs will hold the Japanese weapons until Army and Navy officials decide their disposition.
subfiles.summary: The Department says current procedure normally transfers such articles to Army and Navy custody for examination. They may later be returned to the person entitled to possess them when military authorities consider it advisable.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Charles K. Clark reaffirming import procedure
subfiles.about: Refers Clark to the procedure stated in the Department’s earlier letter.
subfiles.summary: The telegram responds to Clark’s June 13 message. It reiterates that the established procedure for captured weapons remains applicable.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Charles K. Clark on Customs custody
subfiles.about: Tells Clark that Customs will hold the disputed articles pending a decision by the proper authorities.
subfiles.summary: The message answers Clark’s June 4 telegram. It states that a fuller letter will follow.

subfiles.title: Charles K. Clark’s protest against Navy custody
subfiles.about: Challenges a purported Customs letter and objects to the Navy taking possession of his captured weapons.
subfiles.summary: Clark alleges that the signature on a letter attributed to Seattle customs official Oscar W. Dam was forged. He accuses naval personnel aboard the S.S. John Baly of attempting to take his property and cites other merchant seamen whose machine-gun souvenirs were quickly cleared by Customs.

subfiles.title: Senator La Follette’s transmittal of constituent correspondence
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s inquiry about alleged wartime trade with Japan for Department consideration.
subfiles.summary: La Follette asks Hull to give the enclosed communication favorable consideration. He requests a report to accompany the return of the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Ray Henningfeld’s letter concerning alleged trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Questions Walter Judd’s reported claim that the United States was indirectly exchanging supplies with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Henningfeld asks whether U.S. supplies were reaching Japan while Japanese supplies came to the United States, apparently through the Soviet Union. He argues that such trade would undermine civilian sacrifice and war-bond efforts and asks whether Judd’s statement was true or false.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to Senator La Follette on Soviet transit and Japan
subfiles.about: Denies that the United States and Japan were exchanging supplies through the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that no Japanese materials were reaching the United States through Soviet territory and no U.S. materials were going to Japan by that route. It quotes Article III of the June 11, 1942, U.S.–Soviet mutual-aid agreement, which restricted transfer of American defense articles, and encloses the agreement for Henningfeld.

subfiles.title: Nellie Abbott’s inquiry about prewar scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: Asks why scrap iron was shipped from the United States to Japan before Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.summary: The OCR is severely degraded, but the succeeding reply identifies Abbott’s subject as prewar scrap-iron exports to Japan. The letter was sent from Pasadena and referred by the White House to the State Department.

subfiles.title: Reply to Nellie Abbott on restrictions against exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Explains the legal and administrative steps that ended U.S. scrap-iron exports and most trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury says Congress authorized export controls on July 2, 1940, after which strategic commodities and specified scrap grades were progressively licensed and generally denied to Japan. All iron and steel scrap exports to Japan were prohibited from October 16, 1940. The July 1941 freezing of Japanese assets then produced a practical cessation of bilateral trade.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Chilean nitrate exports
subfiles.about: Refers to a Chilean report on nitrate-of-soda exports to Japan and other countries during July–December 1942.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs researchers to Airgram No. 952 from Chile. The report apparently requested verification of export figures and was filed under the Chile defense-materials series.

subfiles.title: Bern follow-up on the Japanese mercury report
subfiles.about: Reports that repeated efforts failed to produce additional details about the proposed mercury transaction.
subfiles.summary: The Legation refers to its May 11 telegram and the Department’s May 6 instruction. Neither the military attaché nor the consuls had obtained information amplifying the original report.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1503 on collection of metal in occupied China
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: Transmits a Chinese press report on Japanese requisitioning of metallic objects in occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson reports that Japanese authorities in coastal occupied China were collecting iron, steel, and brass for war industries. Temple idols and bells, cast-iron gates, household lamps, candlesticks, and Shanghai statues were reportedly removed.

subfiles.title: Japanese Collecting Metallic Articles in Occupied Areas
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese organizations established to requisition metal throughout occupied parts of China.
subfiles.summary: Three committees in Shanghai allegedly searched public buildings and private homes for brass, iron, steel, and reusable waste. The report cites the removal of temple objects, bells, gates, lamps, candlesticks, and landmark statues as evidence of an acute Japanese metal shortage.

subfiles.title: G. C. Evans’s inquiry about prewar scrap shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks why U.S. authorities did not stop scrap-metal shipments to Japan before Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.summary: Evans recalls seeing Japanese ships loading scrap iron and other metals at Gulf Coast ports and San Francisco. He says ordinary citizens foresaw that the material would return in Japanese tanks and guns and asks why the government failed to halt the trade sooner.

subfiles.title: Reply to G. C. Evans on prewar export policy
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Explains the legal limits on discriminatory embargoes and the gradual tightening of controls on exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply reviews the moral embargoes, Neutrality Acts, and the difficulty of denying arms to Japan without also cutting off China. It says the July 2, 1940, export-control authority enabled progressive licensing restrictions, all scrap exports to Japan were denied after October 16, 1940, and the July 1941 asset freeze practically ended trade. Evans is referred to the Department publication Peace and War: United States Foreign Policy, 1931–1941.

subfiles.title: Offer of Japanese ball-bearing catalogues
subfiles.from: I. Fabian Goodman, Bearings Industry Company
subfiles.about: Offers Japanese bearing catalogues and factory information to U.S. military intelligence.
subfiles.summary: Goodman says his company had pre-1940 catalogues from Japanese ball- and roller-bearing manufacturers, some containing factory photographs. He notes that sample Japanese bearings had previously been delivered through Hyatt of General Motors for the Board of Economic Warfare and offers the remaining material to Army or Navy intelligence.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to the Navy on Japanese bearing catalogues
subfiles.to: Commander Frank S. Gary, Navy Department
subfiles.about: Forwards Goodman’s offer of Japanese bearing catalogues to the Navy.
subfiles.summary: Wilson encloses Goodman’s November 6 letter and the Department’s reply. The Navy is invited to contact Goodman directly if the catalogues are useful for intelligence purposes.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to the War Department on Japanese bearing catalogues
subfiles.to: Lieutenant Colonel R. G. McKay, War Department
subfiles.about: Forwards Goodman’s offer of Japanese bearing catalogues to Military Intelligence.
subfiles.summary: Wilson supplies copies of Goodman’s letter and the Department’s acknowledgement. He suggests that the War Department communicate directly with Goodman if it wants the material.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgement of Goodman’s catalogue offer
subfiles.about: Thanks Goodman and states that his offer has been referred to Army and Navy authorities.
subfiles.summary: Wilson says the appropriate authorities have been informed about the Japanese bearing catalogues. They will contact Goodman directly if the catalogues are of interest.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on reported Bolivian arms sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Refers to a report that Bolivia’s governing junta knew of an earlier sale of arms to Japan by the Peñaranda government.
subfiles.summary: Morris Zimmelman of American Rolling Mills was the stated source of the information. The original noon telegram, No. 240, was filed under a separate decimal number.

subfiles.title: Taft memorandum on answering Dow’s magnesium inquiry
subfiles.about: Directs preparation of a high-level legal response to Dow Chemical’s questions about its 1938 magnesium sales.
subfiles.summary: Taft says he and Acheson agree that Hackworth should prepare an answer for the Secretary’s signature. He characterizes the matter as primarily legal and secondarily a question of past departmental policy.

subfiles.title: Handwritten internal note on handling the Dow inquiry
subfiles.about: Comments that the Dow Chemical inquiry should be answered at a senior level.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten text is largely illegible. Its surviving language indicates discussion of the appropriate level and institutional responsibility for answering the magnesium-export question.

subfiles.title: Willard H. Dow’s inquiry about 1938 magnesium exports
subfiles.about: Asks whether Dow Chemical failed any legal or civic duty when it sold magnesium for shipment to Japan in 1938.
subfiles.summary: Dow reports seven shipments totaling 1,525,027 pounds of pure ingot magnesium, placed through a New York concern. After questioning by the Senate Committee investigating the National Defense Program, he asks whether State Department clearance or investigation of the magnesium’s intended use had been required.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply on Dow Chemical’s magnesium shipments
subfiles.about: Explains the licensing law applicable to exports at the time of Dow Chemical’s 1938 magnesium shipments.
subfiles.summary: Hull refers to Section 5 of the 1937 joint resolution and the President’s proclamation defining arms, ammunition, and implements of war. The reply states that no other law administered by the secretary of state required a licence for the magnesium shipments in 1938.

subfiles.title: Senator Byrd’s referral of B. Ellison’s treaty inquiry
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s question about whether a treaty compelled U.S. scrap-metal exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Byrd encloses B. Ellison’s letter from Lynchburg. He asks the secretary for information that will enable him to answer the constituent.

subfiles.title: B. Ellison’s inquiry about a supposed trade obligation to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether a treaty bound the United States to supply Japan with scrap iron, metals, or other commodities.
subfiles.summary: Ellison says he had condemned prewar scrap shipments but was told that a trade treaty required them. He asks Byrd to clarify whether the United States had any such obligation.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Byrd on the 1911 treaty and scrap exports
subfiles.about: Explains the relationship between the 1911 U.S.–Japan treaty and later restrictions on scrap-metal exports.
subfiles.summary: The reply identifies the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation as the likely source of Ellison’s belief. It notes that the United States gave notice terminating the treaty and that it expired on January 26, 1940, after which the government had greater freedom to restrict trade. It adds that licences for all types of iron and steel scrap to Japan were later denied.

subfiles.title: Willard H. Dow’s acknowledgement of Hull’s reply
subfiles.about: Thanks Hull for clarifying the status of Dow Chemical’s 1938 magnesium exports.
subfiles.summary: Dow says his request was intended solely to establish a clear record. He expresses confidence that the 1938 transaction was handled competently.

subfiles.title: Willard H. Dow’s request to publish Hull’s letter
subfiles.about: Requests permission to publish Hull’s April 7 letter and submit it to the Truman Committee.
subfiles.summary: Dow says the Truman Committee’s recent report commented unfavorably on the 1938 magnesium transaction. He asks whether Hull’s exculpatory explanation may be made public and filed with the committee.

subfiles.title: Senator Brooks’s inquiry about scrap-metal exporters and shipping lines
subfiles.about: Requests information on the companies and shipping lines involved in pre-Pearl Harbor scrap-metal exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Brooks relays an inquiry from Ralph L. Hale of Chicago. He asks for the names of sellers and carriers and the date of the final shipment.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Brooks on scrap-metal export records
subfiles.about: Directs Brooks to published tin-plate scrap data and the Foreign Economic Administration for other scrap-export records.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses the National Munitions Control Board’s sixth annual report and notes that tin-plate scrap exports ceased after December 31, 1940. State had no published list of sellers or shipping lines. Records for other scrap metals had passed to the Economic Defense Board and then the Foreign Economic Administration.

subfiles.title: Departmental appraisal of the Japanese armaments report
subfiles.about: Assesses the enclosed intelligence report as valuable evidence of Japanese prewar planning and German technical influence.
subfiles.summary: The note says the report illuminates Japanese military plans and German influence on armaments production. It commends Mr. Boehringer’s initiative and judges the despatch valuable to U.S. military authorities.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2474: Report on Japanese Production of Armaments in 1942
subfiles.about: Transmits a Chinese intelligence document containing monthly statistics on Japanese armaments production in 1942.
subfiles.summary: General Wang Peng-sheng reportedly obtained the material through an agent in enemy territory, with figures purportedly drawn from the Japanese Cabinet Planning Board. The report covers government and private plants in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria and describes German recommendations for rationalizing production. The Embassy warns that totals may be incomplete because major naval bases such as Yokosuka, Kure, and Sasebo are omitted.

subfiles.title: Increased Production of Armaments in Japan
subfiles.doc_type: translated intelligence report with statistical tables
subfiles.from: Chinese intelligence source via General Wang Peng-sheng
subfiles.about: Analyzes German technical assistance to Japan and tabulates monthly 1942 armaments production by major government and private industrial groups.
subfiles.summary: The report describes a German mission headed by Brigadier General Oppenheim that recommended centralized coordination, plant reorganization, underground facilities, and industrial expansion; most proposals took effect on March 1, 1942. It gives commentary on labor, poison-gas production, new facilities in Taiwan and Niigata, and assessments by Tojo and German officers. Tables cover the Tokyo, Kokura, Osaka, Nagoya, Iwahana, Okayama, Hiratsuka, Sakahashi, Mukden, and Pyongyang arsenals, followed by Mitsui, Mitsubishi, and Sumitomo interests, with monthly output of rifles, automatic weapons, artillery, ammunition, tanks, bombs, mines, and explosives. The report continues beyond page 434 in the larger file.
